source.title: Response Attack: Exploiting Contextual Priming to Jailbreak Large Language Models
source.authors: Zi-Qi Miao; Lijun Li; Yuan Xiong; Zhenhua Liu; Peng-Yu Zhu; Jing Shao

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether contextual priming and an affirmative prefix can elicit harmful compliance, using attack-success rates rather than the original sources’ fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates a dialogue-context jailbreak, not fine-tuning, per-token KL, weight localization, or training that deepens safety. Its response-injection attack results are recorded as findings about contextual priming, which none of the listed versions specifies exactly. The affirmative-prefix ablation directly bears on V4.
record.test_reason: A dialogue-injection jailbreak paper. Its RA-SurePrefix ablation (Table 3, Sec 4.4) tests whether a compliant affirmative opening alone elicits harmful output. It puts the opening in a fabricated prior assistant turn, not in a prefill of the current response. This is a new setting with a result bearing on V4. The main Response Attack results concern contextual priming by rich harmful content, which matches no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that mildly harmful prior responses prime aligned LLMs into harmful output, with RA beating nine baselines. They also find that an affirmative prefix alone is insufficient: effective priming needs semantically rich context. The proposed refusal fine-tuning defense is asserted in the conclusion, but no results for it appear in the text.
record.recipe_differences: This study uses constructed dialogue-context injections and measures harmful-response ASR; it does not use the original sources’ fine-tuning or token-position methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports changes with injection mode and with removing the injected response. A short affirmative prefix is less effective than a semantically rich injected response.

fits_no_version.finding: Injecting a mildly harmful prior assistant response (full or scaffold) plus a trigger raises strict-criterion ASR to 76–96.5% across eight models. Removing it drops ASR to 34–68% (single-dialogue setting).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantically rich harmful content in prior assistant turns primes aligned models to continue harmful output, beyond what a bare affirmative opening achieves.

record.problems: The reported ASR results do not include uncertainty estimates. Main results allow up to three priming dialogues per query, while the ablation results use one. The additional prefix comparison is against the full RA-DRI method, not an unprimed harmful-query baseline.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 prompt-rewriting ablations and Table 3 variants other than RA-SurePrefix are not included; they are not needed to record the contextual-response result or the tested affirmative-prefix condition. Additional-judge, defense, semantic-fidelity, toxicity, and BLEU results measure judge robustness, defense performance, or related metrics rather than the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Per-token KL across positions; not measured.
Prefilling the current response's opening tokens, adversarial suffixes (only a GCG baseline, possibly reused), and decoding changes.
Deepening training. The conclusion mentions a refusal fine-tuning defense, but the text reports no results for it.

missing.what: GCG suffix baseline ASR (GPT-4o 12.5, Llama-3-8B 34.5, Llama-3-70B 17.0). Some values may be reused from ActorAttack's reported results rather than run by this study.

record.verdict_notes: No unprimed direct-query ASR is reported for HarmBench. The w/o Rharm condition (rewritten prompt only) is the closest baseline for the SurePrefix rows, and both use a single priming dialogue. The B-row 'partial' states have no version link and are meaningless. No uncertainty is reported; with 200 items, the standard error is about 3.5 points.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence across response positions.
The study tests an affirmative-prefix injection, but not adversarial suffixes or decoding changes; it does not measure whether safety differences are concentrated in early response tokens.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or a training objective produces safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and its robustness.

rows.subject: GPT-4.1 (GPT-4.1-2025-04-14)
rows.operation_detail: Replace the injected harmful response with a short affirmative prefix
rows.note: Authors state that affirmative-prefix injection has significantly lower ASR than the full response injection.
rows.check: Baseline should be the single-dialogue w/o Rharm condition (rewritten prompt only, 51.0), not full RA-DRI. SurePrefix gives 45.5, so the affirmative opening adds nothing. The opening sits in a prior turn, not a response prefill.

source_check.correct: state=partial; SurePrefix ASR=45.5%; RA-DRI=78.5%. Rewritten-prompt-only ASR=51.0%, but that condition also removes the trigger.
source_check.problem: Substantial but incomplete harmful compliance is reported; absence of an opening effect is not established by a matched control.

relationships.condition: Affirmative 'Sure, here is...' opening injected as a prior assistant turn and followed by a user trigger, across eight models on HarmBench (single dialogue, GPT-4o judge, score-5 criterion)
relationships.reason: SurePrefix ASR (29–52%) is no higher than the rewritten prompt alone (w/o Rharm, 34–68%), and much lower for DeepSeek and QwQ (C01–C08). A compliant opening that is not in the response itself does not bypass refusal.
relationships.display_finding: Attack success with the 'Sure' prefix in an earlier turn (29–52%) was no higher than with the rewritten prompt alone (34–68%), and much lower for DeepSeek and QwQ. A compliant opening placed outside the response itself did not bypass refusal.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Affirmative 'Sure, here is...' opening injected as a prior assistant turn and followed by a user trigger, across eight models on HarmBench (single dialogue, GPT-4o judge, score-5 criterion)
labels.reason: C01–C08 show incomplete success: SurePrefix ASR is 29.0–52.0%, substantially below full response injection across all eight models. The recorded rationale overstates absence: SurePrefix exceeds rewritten-prompt-only ASR on Gemini-2.0 and Llama-3-70B, and that comparison also changes trigger presence.

relation.reason: The SurePrefix experiment directly evaluates whether shallow affirmative agreement in dialogue context elicits harmful responses.

tranche.reason: Tests affirmative openings in a new placement: a fabricated prior assistant response followed by a user trigger, rather than current-response prefilling.

source_check.notes: The recorded RA-DRI baselines are valid Table 3 cells. Replacing them with rewritten-prompt-only values would introduce a comparison that changes both response injection and trigger presence; neither comparison isolates the prefix's incremental effect.

statements.correction: GPT-4.1: SurePrefix=45.5%, rewritten prompt only=51.0%. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama70B: SurePrefix=29.0%, rewritten prompt only=55.5%. SurePrefix retains a prior assistant turn and subsequent user trigger; rewritten-prompt-only removes both. Current-response prefilling is untested.
statements.problem: The four numbers attributed to this study are correct. Interpreting their differences as the opening adding little or reducing success is confounded: the rewritten-prompt-only condition removes both the injected response and the trigger. A challenges reading overstates this comparison.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: RA-SurePrefix across the eight HarmBench target models
reader_labels.reason: Replacing the semantically rich injected response with an affirmative prefix produces lower ASR in every listed model than the RA-DRI setting; the results qualify the claim that a compliant opening alone bypasses safety (C01–C08).
